unit.title: Indicators
unit.description: Moving averages, RSI, MACD, Bollinger, ATR, Fibonacci, OBV and VWAP, and their limits

texts: Leo’s whipsaws
Leo
Leo has discovered **moving averages**: the average of the latest closes, drawn on the chart.
My rule: I buy when the price crosses the 20 average upwards and sell when it crosses it downwards.
For weeks, the share moves sideways.
I’ve bought and sold loads of times. I pay commission and *spread* on every one… and I’m losing.
What’s happened to him?
Bad luck: the rule is fine
It’s not luck: in a sideways market, the price crosses the average again and again.
In a sideways market, the average gives false signals
That’s it! The average is flat and every cross is a **whipsaw**, with its own cost.
He should use an even shorter average
A shorter average crosses even more often: more whipsaws.
Averages sum up the past: they confirm the trend **late**.
Simple or exponential
A **moving average** sums up the latest closes. The simple one (SMA) and the exponential one (EMA) do it differently.
Simple average (SMA)
Exponential average (EMA)
Every close in the window carries the same weight
The 50 SMA adds up the last 50 closes and divides by 50.
Gives more weight to recent closes
The exponential one weights what happened most recently more heavily.
Reacts sooner when the price turns
Because recent closes weigh more, it moves before a simple average of the same period.
The 200-session one used as a trend filter
Price above the 200 SMA: long-term uptrend; below it, downtrend.
The 21-session one you can switch on in E-Trading
In E-Trading you have the 20, 50 and 200 simple averages and the 21 exponential.
Sort all five ideas.
The **SMA** weights every close equally; the **EMA** weights recent ones more and reacts sooner. Both **lag behind the price**.
Hint: «exponential» means recent closes count more.
Well done! Both of them lag behind the price.
Simple or exponential? Sort each idea

steps.title: How they’re used
steps.body:
• **Filter:** price above the 200 SMA = long-term uptrend; below it, downtrend.
• **Dynamic support:** in trends, the price often bounces off the 20 or 50 SMA.
• **Slope:** a rising average = uptrend; a flat one = sideways.

And they always arrive late: in sideways markets they give lots of false signals, each with its own commission and *spread*.
steps.key: A moving average smooths the price and shows the trend, always with a delay.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open a chart and turn on the SMA 200.

texts: «Death cross!»
Bruno
Headline: «Death cross on the index!». I’m selling everything.
Bruno is investing for 20 years in an index fund.
Death cross: the 50 average crosses **below** the 200 one.
What do you tell him?
Sell now: the name says it all
The name is scary, but the signal comes late: it’s built from two slow averages.
It’s a late signal and his 20-year plan doesn’t depend on it
That’s it! Changing your plan over a headline usually costs you.
Wait for the golden cross before deciding
The **golden cross** (the 50 above the 200) comes late too.
Let’s see when a real one came, in 2020.
Live through March 2020
Real data: the S&P 500 day by day. You invest **€10,000** on 2 January 2020 and can sell whenever you like, for example on the death cross.
Did the 2020 death cross come before or after the worst day?
Before: it warned in time
After: when the worst was already over
On the same day
The low was on **23 March**; the death cross, on **30 March**, a week later.
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.
Anyone who sold on the cross did so **very close to the low**: by August, the index had already got back to its February high. A cross is a **late snapshot** of what has already happened.
End of the year. Would selling on the cross have done any good?
You’ve sold. Watch what the index does next…
Down 25 %, and the slow averages still haven’t crossed.
Hit «Start». You can sell whenever you like

steps.title: The evidence
steps.body:
Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron (1992) found that simple moving-average rules seemed to work on the Dow Jones from 1897 to 1986. Correcting for data-snooping bias, Sullivan, Timmermann and White (1999) weakened those results considerably, and their predictive power on indices fell or disappeared after 1986.

Its most sensible use: the 200 SMA as a **risk filter** in big downtrends, with whipsaws along the way.
steps.key: Crosses confirm late: they’re more useful as a risk filter than for winning trade by trade.
steps.tip: Try it: open the S&P 500 in Market and turn on the 50 and 200 averages.

texts: Overbought… and still rising
Sara
My share has an RSI of 78. It’s overbought! I’m going to sell it.
What do you tell her?
Well done: above 70, it falls
In strong trends, the RSI can spend **weeks** above 70.
A high RSI says it has risen a lot, not that it’s going to fall
Exactly! Overbought describes the recent past, not the future.
She should wait until it goes above 90
There’s no magic number: the RSI doesn’t say if or when it will fall.
Three weeks later, the RSI is still above 75 and the price is still rising.
Good thing I didn’t sell…
Lots of beginners lose money selling something that just keeps rising.
Good reading or classic mistake
The **RSI** runs from 0 to 100: above 70, «overbought»; below 30, «oversold». Which readings make sense?
Sensible reading
Classic mistake
RSI at 78: I’m selling, it’s going to fall
Overbought isn’t a sell signal on its own.
The RSI spends months between 40 and 80: bullish regime
In uptrends it moves between 40 and 80; in downtrends, between 20 and 60.
The price makes a higher high and the RSI a lower one: the rise is losing steam
It’s a bearish divergence: a clue, not an order.
RSI at 25: a bounce is certain
Nothing is certain: it can keep falling if the slide drags on.
Oversold within an uptrend: an area of interest, with a stop
It’s the most sensible use of oversold: a clue, with a stop.
Bearish divergence: I’m selling everything right now
Divergences can last a long time before the price turns.
Sort all six readings.
A high RSI means **«it has risen a lot»**, not «it’s going to fall». It helps you read the **regime** and divergences, always with a stop.
Hint: be wary of readings with «certain» or «right now».
Very good. The RSI describes; it doesn’t guess.
Sensible reading or mistake? Sort each one

steps.title: What the RSI is
steps.body:
The **RSI** (Wilder, 1978) compares the strength of the gains with that of the losses over the last **14** periods. It runs from **0 to 100**.

• Above **70**: «overbought» (it has risen a lot, without a break).
• Below **30**: «oversold».
• **Bearish divergence:** the price makes a higher high and the RSI a lower one. It can last a long time before the price turns, so it’s never enough on its own.
steps.key: A high RSI doesn’t mean «it’s going to fall»: it means «it has risen a lot».
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, turn on the RSI for a share that has risen a lot.

texts: The cross that came too late
Nico
The share has been rising strongly for weeks. Nico looks at the **MACD**, a momentum indicator built from averages.
The MACD has just crossed upwards! I’m buying now.
What risk is Nico running?
None: the cross says «buy»
The cross says «momentum is improving», not «buy».
The signal arrives just as the move is running out
That’s it! It’s made from averages and inherits their **lag**.
The MACD is miscalculated
The calculation is fine: the problem is that it sums up the past.
And in sideways markets, like the averages, it gives lots of false signals.
What is the MACD saying?
The **MACD** measures momentum with two exponential averages and a signal line. Sort each reading.
Bullish momentum improving
Momentum slowing or bearish
The MACD crosses above its signal line
Bullish momentum is increasing.
The histogram shrinks day after day
The gap between the two lines is narrowing: momentum is slowing.
The MACD is above zero
The 12 EMA is above the 26: uptrend.
The MACD is below zero
The short average is below the long one.
The price rises and the MACD falls
It’s a bearish divergence, as with the RSI.
Sort all five readings.
The MACD is about **momentum**: crosses with the signal line, position relative to zero and the histogram. But it’s made from averages, so it **arrives late**.
Hint: the MACD is the short average minus the long one.
Nice! You can read all three parts now.
Sort each reading

steps.title: How it’s built
steps.body:
Created by Gerald Appel, the MACD (12, 26, 9) has three parts:

• **MACD line:** 12 EMA − 26 EMA.
• **Signal line:** 9 EMA of the MACD line.
• **Histogram:** the difference between the two.

It also has **divergences**, like the RSI. A MACD that crosses upwards says «momentum is improving», not «buy».
steps.key: The MACD measures the trend’s momentum.
steps.tip: Try it: turn on the MACD on a chart in Market and find its latest crossover.

texts: A stop inside the noise
Real bitcoin candles: according to its **ATR**, it moves almost **2 % a day** on average. You buy at the last price: where does the stop go?
If you put the stop 1 % away, less than it moves on a normal day…
It holds: 1 % is plenty
It’ll most likely get hit by pure noise
It doesn’t matter where you put it
A stop inside the normal daily move is almost sure to get hit. Here, any stop less than 2 % away was triggered.
Move the stop out to about 2 times the ATR (4 %) and see what happens.
**Volatility** sets the stop distance: many traders put it at 2–3 times the **ATR**. Inside the normal noise, it gets hit for no reason.
Target hit! This time the noise didn’t knock you out.
Stopped out: that stop was inside the normal daily move.
That stop is closer than the price moves in a day.
Place the stop and hit «See what happened»
Further away, smaller amount
An account of **€10,000** and **1 %** risk: €100. If the stop goes further away, what happens to what you buy?
You move the stop from 2 % to 8 %. To risk the same €100, the position…
Stays the same
Drops to a quarter
Grows fourfold
With the stop at 2 %, the position is **€5,000**; at 8 %, **€1,250**. Four times further away, four times smaller.
Set the stop at 8 % without changing the risk.
The more volatile the asset, **the further away the stop and the smaller the amount**. Your risk in euros stays the same.
Leave the risk at 1 %: what changes is the stop.
Look at the bar: with the stop far away, you buy much less.
Move the stop further away and watch the position

steps.title: Bollinger and the ATR
steps.body:
**Bollinger Bands (20, 2):** a 20-period average in the middle and two bands 2 standard deviations away.
• **When they narrow:** low volatility; it often comes before a strong move (*squeeze*), without saying which way.
• In strong trends, the price can **walk** along the upper band: touching it isn’t a reason to sell.

The **ATR** (Wilder) measures how much the price moves on average, usually over 14 periods. Its **true range** also counts gaps. It doesn’t tell you the direction.
steps.key: Volatility sets the stop distance; your maximum risk sets the size.
steps.tip: Try it: on your next simulator buy, place the stop outside the daily noise.

texts: «Fibonacci never fails»
Laura
Laura has drawn the **Fibonacci retracements**: lines that mark how much of a rise the price gives back.
Look: it rose from €100 to €200 and bounced right at €138.20, the 61.8 % level.
Fibonacci never fails!
What do you tell her?
She’s right: there’s the proof
One case seen in hindsight proves nothing.
With five levels, the price almost always touches one
That’s it! You’d have to test it on lots of cases, not one hand-picked one.
She should use 90 % instead
Changing the number fixes nothing: it’s looking back for whatever fits.
Here, 38.2 % falls at €161.80 and 50 % at €150.
With five lines so close together, the price almost always touches one.
The tool’s levels
After a strong move, the price often **gives back part of it** before carrying on. Which percentages does the Fibonacci retracement mark?
Fibonacci level
Used, but not Fibonacci
Not part of it
It’s the first of the levels.
Closely watched in uptrends.
It doesn’t come from the sequence, but it’s included because it’s widely used.
It comes from the sequence’s 1.618 ratio.
The deepest of the levels.
It’s not part of the tool.
Sort all six percentages.
The retracements mark **23.6, 38.2, 61.8 and 78.6 %** of the move, and **50 %** is added because it’s widely used. They come from the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13…, whose ratio tends towards 1.618.
Hint: the Fibonacci ones have «odd» decimals.
Good. Notice how close together they are.
Sort each percentage

steps.title: Scepticism
steps.body:
There’s no solid proof that these levels work better than other percentages. It may work partly because lots of people place orders there.

A reasonable use: in an uptrend, many people look for buying zones between 38.2 and 61.8 %, especially if they line up with support or an average.
steps.key: Fibonacci organises retracement zones; it doesn’t predict.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, find a strong rise and see where it stopped when it pulled back.

texts: Build the OBV
This share has risen over the week, but were there buyers behind it? The **OBV** checks: it adds the volume of days that **close** higher and subtracts the volume of days that close lower.
Adds its volume
Subtracts its volume
Monday: closes above Friday, with 1,000 shares
Up close: adds 1,000.
Tuesday: opens strongly, but closes below Monday. 800 shares
Only the close counts: subtracts 800.
Wednesday: closes above Tuesday, with 1,500 shares
Up close: adds 1,500.
Thursday: drops mid-session, but closes above Wednesday. 600 shares
What happened during the day doesn’t matter: it closed up and adds 600.
Friday: closes below Thursday, with 1,200 shares
Down close: subtracts 1,200.
Place all five days.
The week’s OBV: 1,000 − 800 + 1,500 + 600 − 1,200 = **1,100 shares**. Its value doesn’t matter: what matters is its **direction** compared with the price.
Look only at the close, not at what happened during the day.
Nice! That’s how it builds up, day by day.
Add or subtract? Look at how each day closes
Below the VWAP
Marta
Marta works at a fund. Today she had to buy a lot of shares in one company.
At the close, my average price ended up below the day’s VWAP.
Did she do well?
Yes: she bought better than the day’s average
That’s it! The VWAP is the volume-weighted average price: her **benchmark**.
No: she should have bought above it
The opposite: buying below the VWAP means buying better than average.
It doesn’t matter: the VWAP is only for predicting
It predicts nothing: it’s for measuring whether you executed well.
It’s the sum of (price × volume) ÷ total volume. It resets every day.

steps.title: The same limits
steps.body:
Both depend on reliable volume data: in forex and crypto, the data are partial. And, like every indicator, they describe what has already happened.

If the price rises and OBV does too, volume is backing the move; if the price rises and OBV falls, there’s a **divergence**: a clue, not a sufficient signal.
steps.key: OBV checks whether volume is backing the move; VWAP shows the average price traded.
steps.tip: Try it: turn on volume on a chart in Market and see whether it backs the move.

u22l1-4.prompt: Match each use of averages with its rule.
u22l1-4.explanation: Averages help you see the trend and its strength, not guess the next move.
right: Price above or below the 200 SMA

u22l1-5.prompt: If you drew an average over these closes, which way would it point? (Nestlé · closes every 3 sessions · January–March 2025)
u22l1-5.explanation: The closes rise steadily: any average would climb behind the price, with a delay.

u22l1-6.prompt: And over these? What slope would the average have? (Procter & Gamble · closes every 3 sessions · November 2025 – January 2026)
u22l1-6.explanation: The price goes back and forth: the average would be almost flat and the price would cross it several times. That’s where whipsaws come from.

u22l1-7.prompt: Picture the 20-session average over these candles. Does the price go up or down over the next 10?
u22l1-7.explanation: An average describes the past with a delay: it doesn’t tell you what will happen over the next 10 sessions.

u22l1-10.prompt: Using the filter rule: long-term uptrend or downtrend?
u22l1-10.explanation: Price above the 200 SMA: long-term uptrend. Below: downtrend. It’s a filter, not a prediction.

u22l1-11.prompt: Your share trades well above its SMA 200, which is rising. It pulls back to the SMA 50 and bounces. How do you read it?
options: Possible support: a clue, with a stop
Sell signal: the price has touched the average
Safe buy: it has touched the average
u22l1-11.explanation: With the price above a rising SMA 200, the 50 average can act as dynamic support. It’s a clue for finding an entry with a stop, not a guarantee.
feedback: That’s it: in trends, the price often bounces off the SMA 20 or 50, but with no certainty.
Touching the average in an uptrend is usually read the other way round: as possible support.
No average guarantees a bounce: the price can cut through it and keep falling.

u22l2-3.prompt: Sullivan, Timmermann and White strengthened the results of moving-average rules.
u22l2-3.explanation: The opposite: by correcting for data-snooping bias, they weakened them considerably.

u22l2-6.prompt: Another real chart, no name. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u22l2-6.explanation: Over 10 sessions, a cross of slow averages has almost nothing to say: it’s designed for trends lasting months.

u22l2-8.prompt: According to the evidence, what has the 200 SMA proved most useful for?
u22l2-8.explanation: It keeps you in during big trends and out of many big falls, with whipsaws along the way.

u22l2-9.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
u22l2-9.explanation: The names are dramatic; sensible use is much more boring.
right: False signal in a sideways market

u22l2-10.prompt: In stretches like this, crosses fail a lot. What trend does it have? (Nestlé · closes every 3 sessions · April–June 2026)
u22l2-10.explanation: In a sideways market, the averages flatten and cross again and again: it’s whipsaw territory.

u22l3-2.prompt: Which zone is the RSI in?
u22l3-2.explanation: The classic thresholds are 70 and 30. Being in a zone describes the recent past, not the future.

u22l3-3.prompt: Price makes a higher high and the RSI a lower high. What is it?
u22l3-3.explanation: The rise is losing steam, but the divergence can last a long time before the price turns.

u22l3-4.explanation: It’s the value Wilder proposed in 1978.

u22l3-5.prompt: In such sustained rises, the RSI usually spends a long time in the upper zone. What trend does this stretch have? (Ethereum · closes every 3 sessions · July–August 2025)
u22l3-5.explanation: Higher highs and higher lows. Selling just because the RSI was high would have meant fighting the trend.

u22l3-6.prompt: No RSI, no name: up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u22l3-6.explanation: Even if you saw the RSI overbought or oversold, it would only tell you how much the price has moved, not where it will go.

u22l3-7.prompt: Another real chart. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u22l3-7.explanation: An oscillator sums up recent momentum; the next stretch may carry on or turn.

u22l4-1.prompt: The MACD line is the 12 EMA minus the ____ EMA.

u22l4-2.prompt: The MACD signal line is a ____-period EMA of the MACD line.
u22l4-2.explanation: It’s the third number in MACD (12, 26, 9).

u22l4-6.prompt: In stretches like this, the short average usually runs above the long one. What trend is it? (Amazon · closes every 3 sessions · March–May 2026)
u22l4-6.explanation: With higher highs and higher lows, the 12 EMA tends to sit above the 26 EMA: positive MACD, with a delay.

u22l4-7.prompt: No indicators in sight. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u22l4-7.explanation: The MACD sums up what the averages have already done: it confirms momentum with a delay; it doesn’t anticipate the next sessions.

u22l4-11.prompt: A share has moved sideways for a month. Its MACD has crossed the signal line five times, up and down. A sixth upward crossover appears. What do you do?
options: I buy double to make up for the earlier whipsaws
I treat it as noise: there’s no trend here
I buy: this time it’s the real one
u22l4-11.explanation: The MACD works in trends. In a sideways market, its crossovers are mostly noise, and every trade has its cost.
feedback: Increasing the size to recover losses is the fastest way to make them bigger.
That’s it: the MACD is built from averages and, like them, fails in sideways markets.
That’s what you thought the five previous times: in a sideways market, crossovers are usually whipsaws.

u22l4-12.prompt: What does each MACD reading say?
options: The histogram shrinks day after day
The price rises and the MACD falls
The histogram grows day after day
The MACD crosses above its signal line
u22l4-12.explanation: Upward crossover and a growing histogram: momentum is improving. A shrinking histogram or a divergence: it’s slowing. No reading tells you what the price will do tomorrow.

u22l5-5.prompt: Place the stop below the recent low, leaving room for the asset’s normal volatility.
u22l5-5.explanation: A stop right at the low gets hit by any wick. Below it and with some room (for example, part of the ATR), it only triggers if the idea really fails.

u22l5-6.prompt: This asset moves a lot. You have €10,000 and risk 1 % at most. Set the stop with some room and adjust the amount.
u22l5-6.explanation: More volatility = stop further away = smaller amount for the same risk. You decide the risk in euros; the market decides the distance.

u22l5-7.prompt: The Bollinger Bands narrow sharply. What does that usually indicate?
options: That the price is going to fall in the coming days
That the price is going to rise in the coming days
That a strong move may be coming
u22l5-7.explanation: The squeeze warns that a move may be coming, not which way.

u22l5-11.prompt: A share’s ATR is €2: that’s how much it moves on a normal day. Is this stop inside the noise or does it have room?
u22l5-11.explanation: A stop closer than a normal day’s move gets hit by pure noise. At 2–3 times the ATR, it’s only hit if the idea really fails.

u22l5-12.prompt: A share is rising strongly and has touched the upper Bollinger Band for five days. A friend tells you: «Touching the band is a sell signal». What do you reply?
options: That she should buy more, because the band guarantees it will keep rising
That touching the band isn’t a sell signal
u22l5-12.explanation: Bollinger Bands measure volatility. Touching the upper one in a strong rise is normal, not a sell order.
feedback: The bands guarantee nothing: they describe how much the price has moved.
That’s it: the bands measure volatility, they don’t mark tops.
In strong trends, the price can walk along the upper band for days: selling because it touches it is going against the trend.

options: Move it away using its ATR and buy less
Yes, remove it: stops only cause trouble
u22l5-13.explanation: Volatility (the ATR) sets the stop distance; the amount adjusts so the risk in euros stays the same.
feedback: Of course: stop outside the noise and a smaller amount. My risk in euros doesn’t change.
Without a stop, one bad trade could cost me more than three small stops.
Closer, it would be hit even more: bitcoin moves much more than that in a day.
lines: I put the stop at 0.5 % on bitcoin.
It’s been hit three times this week. Should I remove it?

u22l6-2.prompt: A share rises from €40 to €60. Where is the 50 % retracement?

u22l6-5.prompt: The 50 % level doesn’t come from the Fibonacci sequence.
u22l6-5.explanation: It’s included because it’s widely used, not because of Fibonacci.

u22l6-6.prompt: A retracement in a rise is drawn from the starting low. Tap it (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · March–May 2026)
u22l6-6.explanation: Here the low is the first close: the levels are spread out from there to the high.

u22l6-7.prompt: In this rise, tap the high of the move: that’s where the retracement would be measured from (Airbus · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2024)
u22l6-7.explanation: The high came before the end and the price was already pulling back. That pullback would be measured as a percentage of the whole rise.

u22l6-11.prompt: A share in an uptrend rises strongly from €40 to €60 and starts to pull back. Near €50, its 50 % retracement, there’s also an old support. How do you use it?
options: I buy everything at €50: Fibonacci guarantees it
I ignore it: Fibonacci is pure magic
I mark it as a zone of interest, with a stop
u22l6-11.explanation: Fibonacci organises retracement zones. It carries more weight when it lines up with other pieces, like a support, and it’s always used with a stop.
feedback: No level guarantees anything: the price can cut through it without stopping.
It doesn’t predict, but it helps organise zones, especially if it lines up with a support.
That’s it: a retracement that lines up with a support is a reasonable zone, never a certainty.

u22l6-12.prompt: Sensible use of Fibonacci or magical thinking?
options: Buying because the price «has to» bounce at 61.8 %
Trying levels until one fits the past
Giving more weight to a level that lines up with a support
Looking for zones between 38.2 and 61.8 % in an uptrend
u22l6-12.explanation: Fibonacci helps organise zones and combine them with other pieces. Believing a level «has to» work, or looking back for the one that fits, is fooling yourself.

u22l7-3.prompt: In one session, 2,000 shares trade at €20 and another 2,000 at €22. What’s the VWAP?

u22l7-4.prompt: Match each indicator with what it measures.
u22l7-4.explanation: Each indicator answers a different question: volume, average price, volatility or momentum.
right: The session’s average price weighted by volume
How much the price moves on average
Cumulative volume depending on whether the day rises or falls

u22l7-5.prompt: Is volume backing the move or is there a divergence?
options: Price at highs and OBV falling
Price at highs and OBV at highs
u22l7-5.explanation: If OBV and the price move in the same direction, volume is backing the move. If they split, there’s a divergence: a clue, not a sufficient signal.

options: Its exact value at each moment
u22l7-6.explanation: The level depends on the day you start counting; what’s useful is the direction.

u22l7-8.prompt: Without seeing volume or OBV, up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u22l7-8.explanation: OBV and VWAP put in order what has already happened with volume. They help you judge whether a move has people behind it, not guess the next sessions.

u22l7-11.prompt: Your share is making new highs, but its OBV has been falling for weeks. What do you do with your position?
options: I take it as a clue: I review my stop
I buy more: new highs are a sign of strength
I sell everything now: the divergence says so
u22l7-11.explanation: If the price rises and the OBV falls, the rise has fewer people behind it. It’s a clue to be cautious, not a sufficient signal to sell.
feedback: That’s it: if volume isn’t backing the move, it pays to be cautious, without treating it as an order.
Highs with volume against them are exactly when more caution pays.
A divergence can last a long time before the price turns, or never turn at all.
